title: Development and preliminary psychometric evaluation of a Narrative Comprehension Assessment (NCA) for Indian children
content:
by Ramandeep Kaur, Darryl Jeethesh Dsouza, Dency Davis, Melicia Shainy Dsouza

Narrative comprehension requires children to understand explicitly presented information and integrate events to derive implicit meanings. Despite its developmental and educational importance, English-language narrative assessments developed within the Indian cultural context remain limited. This study developed and conducted a preliminary psychometric evaluation of the Narrative Comprehension Assessment (NCA), a picture-based assessment for Indian children aged 4–8 years. The NCA was developed across three phases. An initial set of 27 comprehension questions was refined through expert review to 20 items comprising 9 literal and 11 inferential questions. The final assessment used two wordless picture narratives and four sequential components: Picture Walk, Retelling, Prompted Comprehension, and Guided Story Narration. Preliminary evaluation was conducted with 80 typically developing children, equally distributed across four age groups from 4–5–7–8 years. Content validity was high (S-CVI/Ave = 0.93), and internal consistency was high for both narratives (α = 0.97 and 0.96). Significant age-group differences were observed across major NCA components for both narratives (p < .001), with large effect sizes. Literal comprehension exceeded inferential comprehension across all age groups (p < 0.001). Guided Story Narration yielded higher overall scores than Prompted Comprehension for both narratives (p < 0.001). Three-week test–retest reliability was good (ICC = 0.89 and 0.91). The findings provide preliminary evidence for the NCA’s content relevance, internal consistency, developmental differentiation, and temporal stability. Larger and more diverse samples are required to further establish broader psychometric, cultural, and clinical validity and to support future normative development.
